study_identification.title: Detecting accelerated retinal decline in mental disorders through normative modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: To estimate normative variability for the macular region using the largest OCT sample of healthy controls to date (N = 56,545) from the UK Biobank, and to quantify the expected macular thickness decline for the typical UK Biobank age-range (i.e., mid to late age), including its coronal subfields and two of its cellular sublayers (RNFL and GC-IPL). The study then compared age-related retinal decline in individuals with schizophrenia (SZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and major depression (MDD) to the normative decline in healthy controls, hypothesizing accelerated retinal decline in mental disorders.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Spectral domain optical coherence tomography device; automated analysis using custom software developed by Topcon Advanced Biomedical Imaging Laboratory; dual-scale gradient information for rapid segmentation of nine intraretinal boundaries

quality_checking_detail.answer: Image quality control measurements (data fields 28552, 28553: OCT image quality) included. Outlier removal using interquartile range (IQR) trimming approach. IQR multiplier of 4 used in main analysis, which under the assumption of normally distributed variable removes only 0.01% of observations. Outlier removal performed separately within control population and each diagnostic group. Enrichment analysis using chi-squared statistics confirmed no significant differences in outlier observation rate between groups (all χ2 < 1.86, all p> 0.17).

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: UK Biobank is a single-cohort study with standardized OCT measurement procedure. Ethnicity and image quality were included as covariates in the model to account for potential systematic variations.

modeling_method.answer: GAMLSS (Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape); fractional polynomials for non-linear age effects; normal distribution selected based on 5-fold cross-validation

response_variable.answer: Total macular thickness; Macular subfields (inner, central, outer with superior, inferior, nasal, temporal subdivisions); Retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness; Ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GC-IPL) thickness

predictor_variables.answer: Age (fractional polynomials); Sex; Laterality (left/right eye); Image quality; Ethnicity

predictor_effects.answer: Age: fixed effect (non-linear via fractional polynomials); Sex: fixed effect; Image quality: fixed effect (covariate); Ethnicity: fixed effect (covariate). Sex-stratified and laterality-specific models were built for each metric. Interaction effects between sex and age, and between laterality and age/sex were explored.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study handles several important sources of nuisance structure but not comprehensively. Age-related non-linearity is appropriately modeled using fractional polynomials within GAMLSS framework. The GAMLSS approach models both mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ), allowing heteroscedasticity to be captured. Image quality is included as a covariate to account for measurement quality differences. Ethnicity is included to handle population structure. However, the study acknowledges that cardiovascular risk factors and socioeconomic status are only included in robustness analyses and not in the main model, despite known effects on retinal thickness. The justification provided is to maintain comparability with existing literature that did not control for these factors. Additionally, while laterality effects are explored, the main analyses use averaged left-right measurements rather than mixed models accounting for within-subject correlation structure (though this is confirmed in supplementary analyses).
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To model the effects of age on retinal thickness, which are known to be non-linear, we used fractional polynomials which have been shown to provide an accurate method to model nonlinear effects. Image quality and reported ethnic background were also included as covariates, since they have been shown to influence retinal parameters. Although cardiovascular risk factors are also well known to have an effect on retinal thickness, most previous studies on retinal thickness deviations in patients with mental disorders did not have access to the phenotyping depth of the UKBB, and did not take them into account. Thus, we include cardiovascular risk factors and other covariates in our robustness analysis (see Supplementary Results), and not in our main analysis in order to be able to compare our main findings with the existing literature. Similar to previous work on retinal parameters in the UK Biobank we considered the following variables as cardiovascular risk factors, including body mass index (BMI), smoking status, alcohol drinker status, and an ICD-confirmed diagnosis of diabetes mellitus type 1 or 2. Finally, we also considered socioeconomic status (quantified by the Townsend Deprivation Index in the UK Biobank). The GAMLSS approach allows modelling of the entire statistical distribution of phenotype of a variable of interest across the predictor variables. This means that the model not only predicts the mean (μ) across the lifespan but can model changes in standard deviation (σ) and further distribution parameters such as kurtosis (ν) and skewness (τ).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study conducted 5-fold cross-validation (80-20 split) to evaluate different distribution choices for the GAMLSS model and to assess model performance. This represents validation on non-independent but same-domain data (held-out portions of the training dataset). Mean squared error (MSE) was used as the performance metric across folds.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To select the appropriate distribution for our model, we compared the performance of several distributions, quantified by mean squared error, in an 80-20 5-fold cross validation framework (Figure S2). The normal distribution showed equivalent performance to the more complex distributions and was therefore chosen, since it provides the most parsimonious model (see Supplementary Results), and since using the next best performing distributions (generalized gamma or Box-Cox t) provided similar results (not reported).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study conducted a permutation analysis specifically designed to exclude overfitting by training the normative model on a random 80% sample of healthy controls and then comparing the remaining 20% of healthy controls (who were not used in training) to the patient population. This was repeated over 10 iterations. This represents true independent validation within the same domain, as the 20% held-out healthy controls were completely independent from the training data.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: To exclude the possibility that our normative model was overfitting the training data, we performed a permutation analysis. A random 80% sample of the HC population was chosen at each iteration to train the normative models for each metric. Thereafter, normative deviations were compared between the remaining 20% of the healthy control population and the patient population; this circumvents any influence of overfitting since the HC sample compared to the patients has not been used to train the model... Over 10 iterations of the permutation analysis, whereby in each iteration a random 80% sample of the HC sample was used for training, and all subsequent comparisons being made between the remaining 20% of HCs and patients, the average differences on the z-scores of the macular thickness was -0.28 (CI = [-0.37, 0.19], P < 0.0001), for the RNFL metric was 0.08 (CI = [-0.02, 0.19], P = 0.10), and for the GC-IPL was -0.16 (CI = [-0.26, -0.07], P = 0.0012). Similarly, regarding the effects observed within each individual disorder, the results of the permutation analysis showed high agreement with the original analysis.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not validate the normative model using data from a different domain or external dataset. All validation procedures (cross-validation, permutation analysis) were conducted within the UK Biobank dataset. The clinical groups (SZ, BD, MDD) used for comparison were also from the UK Biobank, representing application rather than external validation. No external cohorts or independent datasets from different populations, scanners, or acquisition protocols were used to validate the generalizability of the normative model.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: This analysis used cross-sectional measurements of optical coherence tomography (OCT) from the UK Biobank database (Figure 1A)... To estimate normative retinal decline, we used these measurements from N = 56,545 healthy individuals from the UK Biobank... To relate disease-related retinal decline to the normative decline (Figure 1C), we then included N = 538 separate individuals from the UK Biobank with a mental disorder (Table 1), including SZ (N = 171), BD (N = 265), and MDD (N = 102), according to ICD-10 primary or secondary diagnoses (F20, F31 and F33 respectively).

diseases_studied.answer: Schizophrenia (SZ); Bipolar Disorder (BD); Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores computed from normative model predictions (age-specific predictions adjusting for covariates); averaged z-scores for left and right eye; extreme values defined as |z| > 1.96 SD (infranormal: z < -1.96; supranormal: z > 1.96)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear models (lm in R) with retinal thickness metric deviations as dependent variable and diagnostic group and sex as predictor variables. Mixed models with participant ID as random effect to account for repeated measures (left and right eyes) were used in supplementary analyses. Chi-squared tests were used to assess statistical significance of differences in rate of occurrence of extreme values between groups. Alpha was set at 0.05. Nominal p-values reported without multiple comparison correction. Robustness checks included: (1) permutation analysis with 10 iterations comparing 80% training to 20% held-out HC and patients; (2) linear modeling approach with 250 permutations comparing 1614 resampled HC to 538 patients (3:1 ratio) with Cohen's d effect sizes; (3) extended covariate analysis including BMI, smoking, alcohol, diabetes, and socioeconomic status; (4) sensitivity analyses for patients with lifetime depressive symptoms (N=29,025) vs. stricter ICD-F33 diagnosis; (5) IQR multiplier robustness analysis (range 1-7).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Mental disorders, particularly schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, showed significantly accelerated retinal decline compared to normative age-related decline, with enrichment of infranormal thickness values in macular thickness and GC-IPL, but not RNFL.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Age-related retinal decline was more pronounced across mental disorders compared to healthy controls for total macular thickness (z = -0.29, CI = [-0.35, -0.22], P < 0.0001) and GC-IPL thickness (z = -0.18, CI = [-0.25, -0.11], P < 0.0001), but not RNFL thickness (z = -0.05, CI = [-0.11, 0.01], P = 0.10). The negative deviations were driven by SZ (macular: z = -0.47, CI = [-0.59, -0.35], P < 0.0001; GC-IPL: z = -0.24, CI = [-0.36, -0.12], P = 0.001) and BD (macular: z = -0.23, CI = [-0.33, -0.14], P < 0.0001; GC-IPL: z = -0.16, CI = [-0.26, -0.06], P = 0.004), with significant difference between SZ and BD for macular thickness (Δz = 0.24, CI = [0.14, 0.33], P = 0.0001). MDD showed no significant deviations in any retinal metric. Macular subfield analysis revealed that decline was more pronounced in inner compared to central (Δzavg = -0.13, P = 0.0005) and outer subfields (Δzavg = -0.08, P = 0.01). Disorder-specific differences between SZ and BD were found for outer temporal (Δz = -0.26, P = 0.0022) and outer inferior subfields (Δz = -0.19, P = 0.0288). Extreme value analysis showed significant enrichment of infranormal values: 4.65% of patients vs. 2.03% of HC for macular thickness (X-squared = 17.65, p = 0.0003); 4.83% vs. 2.35% for GC-IPL (X-squared = 13.701, p = 0.0002); but not for RNFL. No enrichment of supranormal values was found. Results were robust to inclusion of cardiovascular covariates, permutation analyses, and different IQR multipliers.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, the study relied on UK Biobank data which focuses on mid- to late lifespan (mean age ~56 years), leaving early-life retinal changes outside the scope of analysis. Second, the cross-sectional design limits ability to track individual trajectories; repeated measurements in the same individuals would provide more comprehensive understanding of age-related retinal decline. Third, cardiovascular risk factors and socioeconomic status were only included in robustness analyses rather than main models to maintain comparability with existing literature, though these factors are known to influence retinal thickness. Fourth, the study is limited to the UK Biobank population, and generalizability to other populations, ethnicities, or scanner types is uncertain.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that the retina can serve as an accessible peripheral marker of neurodegeneration in mental disorders, particularly for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. The findings suggest that structural retinal abnormalities detected through OCT imaging may reflect broader central nervous system pathology. The use of normative modeling provides advantages over traditional case-control approaches by: (1) accounting for healthy variability and its age/sex-related changes; (2) enabling individual-level assessments rather than group-level comparisons; (3) identifying extreme deviations that may be clinically meaningful. The disorder-specific patterns (SZ > BD > MDD) align with known gradients of brain structural alterations in these conditions. Inner macular subfields showed more pronounced differences, potentially reflecting higher ganglion cell density in these regions. The lack of RNFL findings despite GC-IPL thinning suggests pathology may be localized to cell bodies or inner plexiform layer rather than axonal layers. The comprehensive robustness checks (permutation analyses, linear modeling comparisons, covariate sensitivity analyses) strengthen confidence in findings.
